name: One Fish, Two Fish, Red Fish Hamburger

recipe.history:
Redfish — known formally as red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus) — is one of the great culinary treasures of the American Gulf Coast, swimming the brackish estuaries and shallow flats from Texas to Florida for millennia before European contact. Indigenous peoples of the Gulf region, including the Karankawa and Atakapa nations, netted and roasted red drum over open fires long before the fish had a name in English, relishing its firm, sweet white flesh and the way the copper-red scales shimmered like embers in firelight. It was the Creole and Cajun cooks of Louisiana who truly elevated the fish to cultural icon status, folding it into a cuisine shaped by French technique, West African spice traditions, and Spanish pantry staples. The fish reached its modern apex of fame in the 1980s when New Orleans chef Paul Prudhomme introduced blackened redfish to the world — a dish so wildly popular that the species was nearly fished to commercial extinction within a decade, prompting federal catch limits that transformed it from an everyday ingredient into something closer to a prized occasion.

Seafood-inspired flavors first crept into the hamburger universe through the coastal diners and beachside shacks that lined the American shoreline from the mid-twentieth century onward, where the same fryer that turned out fish baskets and shrimp po'boys was never more than an arm's reach from the flat-top griddle pressing beef patties. Cooks began experimenting: tartar sauce ladled onto a cheeseburger, a strip of fried flounder laid across ground beef, Old Bay seasoning dusted into the patty blend the same way it dusted the crab cakes two stations down. Regional traditions like the Maryland crabcake burger, the Pacific Northwest salmon burger, and the Gulf fish-and-beef combo platter all reflect this long conversation between land and sea. The result was not a dilution of either tradition but a new dialect — a burger that carries the salinity and brightness of coastal cooking without surrendering the primal satisfaction of beef, char, and fat. Bob Belcher understands this dialect instinctively, which is why a burger named after a Dr. Seuss rhyme can carry genuine culinary depth.

I first encountered the idea of a red-fish-inspired beef burger on a sticky August evening at a no-name counter joint somewhere outside Biloxi, Mississippi, the kind of place with a hand-lettered menu board and a ceiling fan that moved the heat around without actually cooling anything. The cook — a broad-shouldered woman who ran the flat-top with the calm authority of someone who had done it ten thousand times — offered a "redfish burger" that turned out to be a beef patty seasoned with the same blackening spice blend she used on the fish, topped with a remoulade so sharp and briny it made your jaw tighten pleasantly. I sat on a cracked vinyl stool and ate it in about four bites, then immediately ordered another. There is a particular kind of food memory that does not live in your head but somewhere lower, in the chest or the gut — a warmth that reasserts itself years later when the right smell crosses your path. That burger is one of mine. Every time I mix blackening spice into a patty or drag a spoon through a tangy remoulade, I am briefly back on that stool, with the fan turning lazily overhead and the Gulf somewhere out in the dark beyond the parking lot.

A beef patty cooked to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is not a preference; it is the correct answer to a specific culinary question, and the question is: what is beef actually capable of? Well past that window, myosin proteins have seized, moisture has fled, and what you are eating is a disc of compacted memory of what a burger once was. At medium rare, the fat has rendered just enough to coat every fiber, the exterior carries a proper Maillard crust, and the interior is a yielding, rose-pink, mineral-rich center that reminds you why this particular animal has been at the center of human cooking for thousands of years. It is the temperature at which the beef tastes most like itself. Anything hotter is not food safety — it is anxiety on a plate, and anxiety has no place in a kitchen that takes its craft seriously. Use quality ground beef, handle it gently, trust your thermometer, and pull the patty at 130°F. Rest it. Then build the burger.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, at room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
680g (1.5 lbs) ground beef — 80/20 brisket and short rib blend preferred
1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable) for cooking
1 tsp hot sauce (Crystal or Louisiana brand preferred)
1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
4 slices white American cheese (or mild provolone)
1 medium red onion, thinly sliced into rings
1/2 tsp fine sea salt (for quick-pickled onions)
1 small head green leaf lettuce, leaves separated and washed
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE DOUGH: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Whisk briefly to combine. Add 2 eggs and the warm milk. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes. Increase to medium speed and knead for 5 minutes until smooth.

2. ADD BUTTER TO DOUGH: With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one or two cubes at a time, waiting for each addition to fully incorporate before adding the next — this process takes about 8 to 10 minutes. Once all butter is incorporated, increase speed to medium-high and knead for a further 5 minutes until the dough is smooth, glossy, and pulls away from the sides of the bowl cleanly. The dough will be soft and slightly tacky.

3. FIRST RISE: Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, approximately 1.5 to 2 hours. Alternatively, refrigerate overnight for a slower, more flavorful first rise — remove from fridge 30 minutes before shaping.

4. SHAPE THE BUNS: Turn the risen dough onto a lightly floured surface. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Shape each portion into a tight round ball by folding the edges under and rolling against the work surface with a cupped hand. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Flatten each ball gently with your palm to about 1 inch thick.

5. SECOND RISE: Cover buns loosely with a clean kitchen towel or oiled plastic wrap. Let proof at room temperature for 45 to 60 minutes until visibly puffed and pillowy. Meanwhile, preheat oven to 375°F / 190°C.

6. BAKE THE BUNS: Beat the remaining egg with 1 tablespoon of water. Gently brush the top of each bun with egg wash. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 15 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing — at least 30 minutes.

7. MAKE THE BLACKENING SPICE BLEND: Combine smoked paprika, sweet paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, dried oregano, dried thyme, cayenne, salt, black pepper, and white pepper in a small bowl. Stir thoroughly to combine. Store any extra in an airtight jar.

8. MAKE THE CREOLE REMOULADE: Combine mayonnaise, Creole mustard, lemon juice, horseradish, hot sauce, Worcestershire sauce, and grated garlic in a medium bowl. Stir until smooth. Fold in the chopped dill pickles, capers, and parsley. Season with smoked paprika, cayenne, and a pinch of salt. Taste and adjust heat or acidity as needed. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld — up to 3 days in advance.

9. QUICK-PICKLE THE RED ONIONS: Combine white vinegar, water, sugar, and salt in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until sugar and salt dissolve. Place sliced red onion rings in a heatproof jar or bowl and pour the hot brine over them. Let cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 20 minutes. Pickled onions will be bright pink and pleasantly sharp.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Remove ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g each). Handle as little as possible — overworking develops gluten and makes patties dense and tough. Gently form each portion into a round patty about 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than your buns (they will shrink when cooking). Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb — this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks. Season both sides generously with sea salt and black pepper.

11. APPLY BLACKENING SPICE: Dust the top side of each patty with a moderate, even coating of the blackening spice blend — approximately 1/2 teaspoon per patty. Do not rub it in; let it sit as a crust on the surface.

12. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a large cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Add neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place patties spice-side-down in the skillet. Do not press down. Cook undisturbed for 3 to 3.5 minutes until a deep, blackened crust has formed. Flip once and cook for a further 2 to 2.5 minutes. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — target is 130 to 135°F / 54 to 57°C for medium rare. Remove patties from heat immediately at 130°F; carryover cooking will bring them to 133 to 135°F during the rest.

13. ADD CHEESE AND REST: Place one slice of American cheese on each patty immediately after flipping, so it begins to melt during the final minutes of cooking. Once pulled from the heat, tent loosely with foil and rest for 3 to 4 minutes. Do not skip the rest — it is the difference between a juicy burger and a dry one.

14. TOAST THE BUNS: While patties rest, melt butter in the same skillet over medium heat. Place buns cut-side-down and toast for 60 to 90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped. Remove and set cut-side-up.

15. BUILD THE BURGER — BOTTOM TO TOP: Spread a generous tablespoon of Creole remoulade on the cut face of the bottom bun. Layer with 2 to 3 leaves of green leaf lettuce, followed by 2 tomato slices. Place the rested, cheese-draped patty on the tomatoes. Top with a small tangle of pickled red onions and 2 bread-and-butter pickle chips. Spread a thinner layer of remoulade on the cut face of the top bun. Set the top bun in place, press gently, and serve immediately.
